sources.title: The Great Fire of 1834
sources.locator: The Great Fire of 1834; Fire!; Did you know?
sources.summary: Two cartloads of obsolete tally sticks were burned in underfloor stoves below the Lords. Visitors noticed heat and smoke but work continued. Furnaces extinguished at 5pm; alarm at 6pm. Both chambers and most site buildings destroyed; Westminster Hall and other parts survived. Split tallies served medieval accounting.
limits: Institutional historical synthesis, not an eyewitness transcript.
The blaze followed a chimney fire; not a claim that sticks directly touched the chamber floor.
Most of the old Palace, not all Parliament or the present Victorian building.

sources.title: Tally Sticks
sources.summary: Tallies were receipts for government income originating in the Middle Ages. Residual two cartloads after abolition in 1826; Clerk of Works chose furnace disposal rather than open-air burning or firewood distribution. Catalogue identifies genuine medieval tallies c1293-1294 as similar examples, not the destroyed 1834 batch.
limits: Correlated with Parliament fire account; not independent institutional corroboration.
Catalogue objects are surviving examples, not sticks recovered from the fire.

sources.title: Payments through time
sources.summary: Notches represented the recorded debt; splitting lengthwise gave each party a record. Museum example records one of the Bank’s earliest government loans in 1694.
limits: Debt example corroborates split-record mechanism, not every government payment procedure.
No monetary value or Bank loan date is narrated.

sources.title: The Fire of 1834 and the Old Palace of Westminster
sources.locator: PDF pages 2–3 (A Georgian Conflagration), page 10 (Westminster Hall)
sources.summary: Chimney fire smouldered under the Lords floor following burning of two cartloads of obsolete receipts in heating furnaces. Warnings ignored; flames emerged through floor after six. Vulnerable sprawling building and firefighting conditions mattered. Westminster Hall was protected and survived.
limits: Parsed PDF and page 2 screenshot inspected; no artwork reproduced.
Same institution as other fire sources; no false independence claim.
Furnace/flue geometry, flame timings and trajectories in visuals are qualitative schematics.

definitions: The 1834 Palace of Westminster fire resulted from furnace disposal of obsolete wooden tally receipts.
Established institutional historical account; dangerous disposal in a vulnerable building, not accounting itself.
Government tallies recorded financial transactions with notches and were split to give matching records.
Receipt and debt uses varied; schematic notches represent no exact monetary amount.
Two cartloads of obsolete tallies remained for disposal in 1834.
Historical approximate volume; carts shown represent the stated two loads, not measured mass.
Workers burned the tallies in heating furnaces beneath the House of Lords.
Simplified cutaway, not a surveyed furnace/flue plan.
A chimney fire smouldered below the chamber floor; heat and smoke were noticed but the disposal continued.
Compresses documented afternoon sequence; no invented motives, dialogue or precise combustion model.
Flames emerged through the House of Lords floor that evening.
No explosion mechanism or minute-level time claimed.
Both parliamentary chambers were destroyed, while Westminster Hall survived.
Other parts also survived. Old Palace, not present Big Ben/new Palace.
The entire Palace of Westminster was destroyed.
lines: In 1834, Britain’s Parliament caught fire because workers were destroying old receipts.
For centuries, the government recorded payments with notches, then split the wood so both sides kept a matching record.
When that system became obsolete, two cartloads of sticks were left to dispose of.
Workers fed them into heating furnaces beneath the House of Lords.
A chimney fire smouldered under the chamber floor. Heat and smoke were noticed, but the burning continued.
Both parliamentary chambers were destroyed. Westminster Hall survived.
The dangerous part wasn’t keeping records on wood. It was choosing where to burn them.

Macro view of one original notched wooden tally; no currency claim.

Chambers darken to damage silhouettes while labelled Westminster Hall remains standing; other survival not denied.
